title: Army’s planned Iowa blast raises questions about aging military stockpiles
text:
Army’s planned Iowa blast raises questions about aging military stockpiles
Despite protests, the U.S. Army plans to detonate tons of unstable military explosives, while also looking at safer alternatives for the future.
The U.S. Army plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives in Iowa on Wednesday, despite public protests and what the service acknowledges are “known risks to human health.”
The controlled explosion of lead azide would send toxic dust into the air that is likely to settle on cars, houses, and playgrounds, military officials said in a letter to residents of Middletown, Iowa.
It urged them to close windows and stay indoors if they are unable to evacuate beforehand, and to make a plan to clean up afterward.
The U.S. Army plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives in Iowa despite public protests. It’s raising questions about how to keep the public safe while also fulfilling the military’s needs.
Lead azide makes bullets and other armaments detonate on demand and has been at the “heart” of military weapons, as the Army puts it, for decades. But supplies have degraded and become unstable over time, making it unsafe to either move or chemically treat them safely.
Along with public safety concerns, the detonation also raises questions about how the military should dispose of dangerous chemical substances, as well as the need to find alternatives that carry fewer risks.
The courts stepped in last week following an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, temporarily suspending a government permit authorizing the Army to carry out the plan.
The Trump administration responded that the U.S. military didn’t need that permit and could proceed anyway. The Justice Department said the detonation needed to be done quickly: “As the outside temperatures drop the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases.”
By Monday, President Donald Trump said he would delay the detonation until the courts made their decision. Later that day, a three-judge federal appeals court panel ruled that the Army could proceed.
Search for a safer alternative
The military has long been aware of the potential health risks of lead azide. But because it’s been so reliable, interest in finding alternatives has “historically been muted,” according to a U.S. Army report this month.
Supply chain disruptions and a limited domestic manufacturing base mean that American troops “must rely on aged stockpiles” for supplies, it added.
This, along with lead azide’s instability, toxicity, and environmental risks has, in recent years, convinced the Pentagon to search for substitutes.
This month, it announced that an alternative safer chemical compound is showing promise. It’s a copper-based mixture known as DBX-1, which has been found after “several years of rigorous testing.”
It’s said to be easier to manufacture and transport, which has piqued the interest of mining companies as well. A full-scale pilot plant could be ready within about a year.
Army advice to the public
For now, the detonation of toxic lead azine in Middletown, Iowa, is set to go ahead as planned.
It will be blown up “inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete” and surrounded with barriers approximately two stories high filled with sand, according to the Army letter.
The soil above will be “thoroughly saturated with water,” it adds, a measure that “should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation.”
The letter goes on: “Extensive modeling efforts predict that the potential level of lead particles in the air may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA [Environmental Protection Agency] would require protective actions be taken.”
The detonation will, nonetheless, “result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground.”
People living nearby are being advised to evacuate or stay inside. The Army says that they should also “consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces” afterward, including playgrounds, tables, chairs, decks, toys, and other items, the letter advised, that children are likely to touch.
